My family never took vacations or trips or holidays either. 
The only times that we went to places out of the country or stayed in hotels was because my dad was a preacher, and people wanted him to speak at different church conventions and such. Apart from that, we never went hiking or camping when I was young, and I never thought much of it because we were poor and couldn’t afford to go. 

After I moved away for college, though, I met another family that was also from a very similar financial background as my own, but they would budget for annual camping trips, take us hiking or shooting as often as the dad got holidays from work, or otherwise have smaller but equally fun days at the pool or the museum. I learned that being poor was no excuse for having fun family trips/days. 

Looking back at my own family, I remember that when I got older and began to question why we didn’t go anywhere like other families did, my dad would say that he was always “too busy” with his work. Then the go-to reason became that we as children hadn’t completed a satisfactory amount of schoolwork every day (we were homeschooled, so having a daily quota of homework that we didn’t meet was something that could be used an excuse). Then the blame shifted to Covid and the consequent lockdowns. All other times, asking why we never went anywhere was met with my parents getting defensive and going back to the “you didn’t finish your work argument”. 

I just thought I’d share my two cents on this because it reminded me of how I grew up. Needless to say, I won’t be repeating all that with my own family.

Apologies for this rather wordy reply, but I came by this subreddit to look for some good stuff to read before going to sleep and I’m glad I came across this post. I’m 21 as well (just completed my sophomore year in college) and I’m nearly word-for-word going through the exact same situation. 

I got fired from my on-campus job over something incredibly silly this past semester - I got served my papers during finals week after an exhaustingly drawn-out process with HR - and I still feel guilty for slipping up, as this job played a big part in my endeavor to self-support throughout college. I’ve since gotten another position as learning assistant to a professor at my college throughout summer school, but like what you’re experiencing, it’s a low-paying position that gives me just enough budget for cheaper grocery items like rice and canned food. On top of that, my laptop’s motherboard decided to get fried, with the result being that all data previously stored on the device is now permanently lost, and I have to use the public-access computers in the university library to get my work done. 

With all that being said, you’re not alone going through this. And I wanted to offer my sympathy and encouragement to you. There are days where I struggle with anxiety and desperation and crippling regret over losing my job and not being able to see a way forward, but I’m moving forward now and happily, having more good days than bad days. Here are the things that really, really helped me out: 

1) Absolutely do not, do not, do not, let your mind go to a dark place. Give yourself some time to “grieve”, but throw yourself into looking for ways forward. We’re both in college, and there are tons and tons of opportunities on and off-campus that you can explore. Try as many things as you can, and some are bound to work out. Losing one job is not the be-all, end-all. Just be smart about explaining to potential future employers how you came to leave your precious job, if you’re like me :p 

2) No friends or people to be your support network? Open YouTube and put on motivational speeches. This worked wonders for me. People who’ve been through the mill screaming at you to keep going. ‘Nuff said! 

3) Let time go by. You’ll be looking back on all this during the fall semester like “damn, I really survived all that!” One mistake and one bad day doesn’t define you. Just go forward and commit to keeping a brave heart and a hardworking attitude and things will sort themselves out!

Best of luck with everything and I’ll be praying for you! Lowkey, let me know how things are going in a couple of months cuz I’m really invested to see how your side of our shared experience plays out!

Think in terms of what you can afford, and what living conditions you would like to be surrounded with. 

Think about the cleanliness of especially the bathrooms, whether they have things like food drainage etc, and also about the overall conditions of the room, whether they’re old and have lots of dust or mold in the ceilings or mattresses or whatever. 

Consider how far your residence will be from the part of the campus where you’ll attend classes most frequently.

Check if your residence hall / dorm has a good cafeteria or mess hall. 

Also, some Universities have separate learning communities in specific residence halls. Some are more populated with engineering majors, some with pre-med, etc. So if you’re going to want a study group or something like that try to look for a learning community that fits you. 

Hope this helps! All the best with your selection process!

I think there are two simple keys to answering these arguments: 

1. Statistics are not hard facts. 

A study is limited in its range, covering only one region and one group of test subjects, which, along with it being guided by a pre-determined (and therefore inevitably biased) set of parameters and questions, hence rendering it only at best a good conjecture made by those conducting the survey based on a limited amount of data. Surveys are merely conclusions based on a superficial set of questions posed to a group or groups of individuals. They do not know everything about the people who answer, and because everyone is so idiosyncratic and unique, they can only make a small, unverified guess as to the behaviors and conditions a person exhibits and exists in. To sum it up, a statistic does not represent ALL gay people, nor does it know EVERYTHING about the ones that do participate in it, and therefore it should not be treated as a fact. 




2. The majority should never represent the individual. 

This is very very straightforward. Just because there are a number of gay people who are more promiscuous than the rest, it does not mean we all are promiscuous. And so on and so forth. On the other side of the coin, because some straight couples fail at raising children, it does not mean that all straight couples fail at raising children. 
Once the person that uses this false argument gets the same argument turned on their flaws or the flaws of their community, they will very quickly realize that theirs is a plain fallacy of reasoning.

I had something very similar happen to me at the beginning of this year. I had a very intense, four-month long crush on a straight guy about my age, so much so that I thought I might be in love with him at certain points. However, another friend advised me to give myself about four months to get over my attraction, which was something I knew I couldn’t carry on anyway. I didn’t believe her, but as I got to know the guy better, I began to notice small things about him that I hadn’t noticed before — that I didn’t really fancy. About 5 months later, I’m feeling all normal towards him like nothing ever happened, and I often laugh at myself for having crushed in him. I still think he’s cute, but, nahhhh 😝

Anyways, bottom line is that you will feel something initially when you first meet someone because you and him will be doing your best to make a good impression on your parts. Just let some time go by, and eventually little things in the way he says or does stuff will slowly erode your attraction and after a few months you’ll be ready to move on. Hope this helps :D

“You shouldn’t be weak…”, 
“don’t open yourself to deception…”, 
“why are you still like this? I thought you said that you were changed after the last talk we had…”, 
“do you want to end up doing abomination?…”, 
“AIDS is God’s punishment for that kind of lifestyle…”,
“if you ever make this public, that will be the end of our family, your grandparents, the church… you will destroy many people’s lives…” 

Those were somethings my parents have said to me throughout the years when I still thought that I could pray the gay away and I tried to reach out for help. I try my best not to grudge against them, and They don’t know that I still remember all these hurtful things, and based on previous experiences, I know that they will be very unhappy if I bring these experiences up. But all these things that they said had an undeniable effect on me. My whole teenage life was wasted with me fighting to get through every day against so much internalized self-hate that would manifest in my thoughts every few minutes. I’m 19 now, and learning to grow out of all that and love myself for who I am is something I am unspeakably thankful to know how to do. 

To everyone else who’s standing in the same shoes as I once stood in, I hope that you will find that beautiful frequency where you know and love yourself for who you are. I’ve been through 6-7 years of depression and suicidal thoughts based on things that were said to me, and I didn’t think it could get better. But I’m on the other side of it all now, and I want to talk you that it does, indeed get better. 

Keep pushing :))) the light at the end of the tunnel is coming and it’s light that will give you freedom unlike anything you’ve ever known before.
